Along with your income and debt status, your personal credit profile can have a significant impact on which loans are available to you and the rates offered. A high credit rating can save you thousands of dollars over the life of a loan.
Individuals with excellent credit ratings typically have a FICO score above 740
Individuals with good credit ratings typically have a FICO score between 660 and 740
Individuals with fair credit ratings typically have a FICO score between 580 and 660
Individuals with poor credit ratings typically have a FICO score below 580

Your FICO score (an acronym for the credit scoring service, Fair Isaacs Company) is an assigned number between 300 and 850 that indicates to lenders your capacity to repay a loan. It can change regularly, as new information is sent by your creditors to one or more of the three major national credit bureaus, Experian, Trans Union, and Equifax. The higher your FICO score, the more likely you will qualify for a mortgage loan and the best interest rates.
A FICO score is comprised of 5 parts:

Your types of accounts and your payment record; any bankruptcies, legal judgments, wage garnishments, etc.; the severity and amount of late payments; the number of past-due items and when they occurred. (35%)
How much you currently owe and on what types of accounts; number of accounts with balances; the proportion of credit lines still available. (30%)
Time since accounts opened; by specific type of account; since last activity. (15%)
Number of recently opened accounts, by type and date opened; recent credit inquiries and date of inquiries; reestablishment of good credit after payment delinquencies. (10%)
The number and types of credit accounts available for your use. (10%)
By federal law, you're entitled to a free credit report once every 12 months from each of the three major credit bureaus - Experian, TransUnion, or Equifax.

waitForText.value: Make Smart Use of Your Credit Card

verifyText.value: Putting the following good habits into practice can help you take control of your finances and boost your credit rating.

If you can't pay a card balance in full each month, review your budget to determine how much you can earmark for that payment without sacrificing other important goals, such as saving for retirement. Making minimum payments on one card can make sense if it's part of a strategy to pay off higher interest rate cards first.

Be proactive and reduce the risk of fraud by regularly reviewing your monthly credit card statements and checking your account online. Notify your card issuer promptly if you spot any erroneous or unrecognized transactions.
Keep spending in check with balance alerts

Set up balance alerts so that you'll be notified by text and/or email whenever your total spending hits a certain threshold that you've set. Keeping your credit card balance under 30% of your limit positively impacts your credit score.
Don't close your only - or oldest - credit card

While missing a payment or carrying a large balance can lower your credit score, so too can canceling an older card or closing down an account that you rarely use. This is especially true if the credit card is the only active credit account you have or your oldest credit card account. Leaving your only (or oldest) credit card open with a $0 balance shows to lenders that you have experience managing various types of credit accounts, and the longer that history the better.

waitForText.value: Which Rewards Program is Best for You

verifyText.value: Cash back. Free hotel stays. Free or upgraded flights. Figuring out which rewards card will deliver the best payoff for your lifestyle and personal spending patterns can seem daunting. Which factors should you consider before applying for a rewards credit card?

The most popular and straightforward reward is cash back. With a cash back reward program, a percentage of the amount that you spend is paid back to you. Some programs have higher pay back rates in specific categories (e.g. gas, grocery stores, restaurants, etc.) while others offer a flat rate regardless of spending category. Other reward programs give you a certain number of miles or points for purchases that you can redeem for free travel, gift cards, merchandise, or other perks. Savvy consumers that have the patience, discipline, time or flexibility to hunt out the best redemption opportunities can get incredible deals on these cards.

Other reward programs give you a certain number of miles or points for purchases that you can redeem for free travel, gift cards, merchandise, or other perks. Savvy consumers that have the patience, discipline, time or flexibility to hunt out the best redemption opportunities can get incredible deals on these cards.

Some cards have huge sign-up bonuses - typically in cash back, points or miles - if you meet the spending requirements within a specific timeframe to qualify for them. These awards can be worth hundreds of dollars in value.

Credit cards come with multiple fees - some are worth paying, others aren't, and most are avoidable. The most common credit card fees include annual fees, balance transfer fees, foreign transaction fees, late payment fees, and cash advance fees. Cards with annual fees tend to have higher rewards structures and higher signup bonuses than those without, so they're worth considering. If you travel overseas at all, you should get a credit card without foreign transaction fees.

Rewards based credit cards are more beneficial to consumers who pay their credit card statement off every month. These cards generally have higher Annual Percentage Rates (APRs) and if the balance were not paid in full every month, the extra interest would eclipse any rewards earned.
